questions.q: In BAI2, which numeric range generally represents debit (money-out) summary and detail codes?
questions.explain: 401-699 are debit summary and detail codes, following 400 (total debits summary); 101-399 are the credit equivalent.

questions.q: What does BAI2 code 455 typically represent?
questions.explain: Code 455 indicates a returned ACH item — a credit that was reversed, which needs different handling than a normal deposit.

questions.q: Why does Oracle need a configured mapping for each bank's transaction codes, rather than just storing the raw code?
options: Because raw codes cannot be stored in a database field
Because the mapped meaning drives downstream behavior like matching rules and classification
Because every bank uses identical codes already
Because mapping is only needed for CAMT.053 files
questions.explain: The mapped meaning determines which matching rules apply, how a line displays, and how it's handled downstream — the raw code alone isn't enough.

questions.q: What is the best description of an 'unmapped' transaction code?
options: A code that causes the entire statement file to be rejected outright
A code that automatically reconciles itself
A code reserved only for CAMT.053 files
A setup gap where no mapping has been configured for that bank-specific code
questions.explain: An unmapped code signals a configuration gap — the fix is to add the mapping once, not to repeatedly fix individual statement lines.

questions.q: Why might two different banks send what is functionally the same transaction (an ACH credit) under different codes?
options: Banks are required to use identical BAI2 code sets by law
Banks aren't perfectly consistent with each other in how they assign codes
Oracle assigns the codes, not the bank
ACH credits cannot appear on a BAI2 statement
questions.explain: Different banks can use different codes for similar transactions, which is exactly why a configurable mapping per bank is necessary.
